page.title: Research record
page.purpose: Every idea we tested, how we tested it, and why only one book survived.
page.standards: Every test used point-in-time data, fills at the next day's open, 7 bps a trade and walk-forward training, and we count every trial.
page.survived_note: Two versions of one book. 1.3 is the live paper book; 2.1 is the same book sized by a volatility forecast, tracked beside it from the same start.
page.chart_note: Growth of $100 from the same day. Book lines are backtests until the paper tracks start on 2026-06-02. 2.1 has forecasts from 2012 and sizes like 1.3 before that; it is dashed until its forecasts were recorded live.
page.demo_link: See how the vol forecast sizes positions
page.tested_note: One row per idea, newest first within each verdict. Select a row to see how we tested it.
page.trust_lead: Test enough random strategies and one will look good by luck. This is how good a lucky one looks after {n} tries, and where our ideas landed.
page.book_lead: Changes to the book are measured as the change in its Sharpe, so they sit on their own scale. Since v49 a change needs at least a 0.90 chance that the gain is real, with drawdown no worse; earlier changes used bars set before each test.

rows.name: Trend + Carry 1.3
rows.why: Trend and carry lose money at different times, so the blend is steadier than either.
rows.expected: Trend following and carry are two of the best-documented premia across asset classes, and they tend to pay at different times. A small book of liquid ETFs should capture both.
rows.how: We built it in steps from v29 to v44, and each part had to pass on its own before it went in. Fills are at the next day's open with 7 bps a trade, on about 23 ETFs from 2007.
rows.happened: The full book earned a Sharpe of 1.24 from 2007 with a worst drawdown of −12.5%. Changing any one setting of the base blend kept Sharpe between 0.93 and 1.12.
rows.works: Trend makes its money in long sell-offs and carry in calm markets, and they correlate at +0.13. A small classifier skips weak trend entries and a rule halves exposure in falling, volatile markets. None of it predicts returns.
rows.mind: A forward record that falls well below the backtest's 5th-percentile path.
rows.citation: Hurst, B., Ooi, Y. H. & Pedersen, L. H. (2017). A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing. Journal of Portfolio Management 44(1).

rows.name: Regime de-risk
rows.why: Halving exposure in falling, volatile markets halved the worst drawdown.
rows.expected: Trend's worst losses come in sharp equity reversals. We can't predict those, but we can react once the market is both below its long-term average and volatile.
rows.how: When SPY is below its 200-day average and its 21-day volatility is above 20%, the book runs at half size. We tested 7 versions of the rule and nearby thresholds.
rows.happened: Sharpe rose from 1.222 to 1.250 and the worst drawdown fell from −10.5% to −5.4%. The drawdown stayed at −5.4% for every nearby threshold.
rows.works: It reacts after a sell-off has started instead of guessing when one will. It fired in 53 episodes over 18 years, so it costs little to run.
rows.mind: A forward stretch where the rule fires often and the book still falls more than before.
rows.citation: Moreira, A. & Muir, T. (2017). Volatility-Managed Portfolios. Journal of Finance 72(4).

rows.name: Meta-label filter
rows.why: A small classifier skips the weakest trend entries. Bigger models did worse.
rows.expected: Meta-labeling leaves the trading rule alone and trains a model to decide which of its signals to act on. That suits a market where returns are mostly noise.
rows.how: We labelled every trend entry from 2007 by what happened next and retrained the model walk-forward with purged folds. We tried 8 versions.
rows.happened: Out of sample the model was right only a little more often than a coin (AUC 0.541). Dropping the worst-looking entries still lifted book Sharpe from 1.041 to 1.226.
rows.works: A depth-2 model beat deeper ones, because with this little signal a bigger model fits noise. It only removes trades, so a wrong call costs a missed entry, not a new position.
rows.mind: An out-of-sample AUC that falls to 0.5 in the forward record.
rows.citation: López de Prado, M. (2018). Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley.

rows.name: Carry and defensive sleeve
rows.why: Steady income in calm markets, where trend struggles.
rows.expected: Assets with a higher yield tend to earn more than their price change suggests. A long-only income book tilted by the yield curve should earn that premium in calm markets.
rows.how: Bonds, credit and gold in risk-parity weights, leaning into duration when 10-year yields sit well above 3-month yields. Monthly rebalance at the next open, 7 bps.
rows.happened: On its own it earned a Sharpe of 0.98, higher than trend's 0.67. It correlated with trend at +0.13.
rows.works: It has no defence in a long sell-off, but trend does, and they rarely lose together. Blended by risk the two reached 1.03 from 2007.
rows.mind: Carry and trend starting to lose in the same months.
rows.citation: Koijen, R., Moskowitz, T., Pedersen, L. H. & Vrugt, E. (2018). Carry. Journal of Financial Economics 127(2).

rows.name: Cross-asset trend
rows.why: The first idea that worked. It gained 7.1% in 2008 while SPY fell 43.4%.
rows.expected: Assets that have been rising tend to keep rising for a while, across stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies. The effect has paid in most long sell-offs.
rows.how: Each ETF's position is the average sign of its 3-, 6- and 12-month returns, scaled so every asset carries the same risk. Monthly rebalance at the next open, 7 bps.
rows.happened: Sharpe 0.67 from 1994, and it beat SPY in 4 of 5 crisis windows. It gained 7.1% in 2008 while SPY fell 43.4%.
rows.works: Because it can go short, it gains when a sell-off lasts. It loses in fast reversals like 2020, which the regime de-risk was later built for.
rows.mind: Several long sell-offs in a row where trend fails to gain.
rows.citation: Moskowitz, T., Ooi, Y. H. & Pedersen, L. H. (2012). Time Series Momentum. Journal of Financial Economics 104(2).

rows.name: Trend + Carry 2.1
rows.why: The same book, sized by a volatility forecast instead of the 60-day window.
rows.expected: The book sizes each ETF by its last 60 days of volatility, so a position stays large until a shock is already in the data. A forecast of the next 21 days should react sooner.
rows.how: An XGBoost model reads recent and intraday-range volatility, the VIX curve and Fed meeting dates, trained on 23 ETFs since 2006. We scored it on held-back data from 2023-11, then froze it on 2026-10-30.
rows.happened: On held-back data the forecast beat the 60-day window by 27.5% (p 0.00076). In the book it lifted development Sharpe from 0.898 to 0.947 but missed the 2018 Q4 check by 0.008, so it wasn't deployed.
rows.works: The forecast is clearly better, but the gain in the book is small and not yet confirmed. It now runs as a paper track next to 1.3, with forecasts recorded each morning before the open.
rows.mind: A forward record where the forecast stops beating the 60-day window, or where 2.1 falls clearly behind 1.3.
rows.citation: Christensen, K., Siggaard, M. & Veliyev, B. (2023). A Machine Learning Approach to Volatility Forecasting. Journal of Financial Econometrics 21(5).

rows.name: Month-end stock and bond spread
rows.why: Real before costs. A 28 bp round trip took all of it.
rows.expected: Balanced funds sell whatever rose more during the month and buy the laggard near month-end. Trading against that flow should pay.
rows.how: Five sessions before month-end we compared SPY's and IEF's returns for the month and bet on the laggard. We then judged it only on data no one had seen: 1993 to 2002 and 2023 to 2026.
rows.happened: The unit spread averaged +34 bp before costs, but the equal-risk trade lost (net Sharpe −0.33). On unseen data it averaged −0.6 bp a trade after costs.
rows.why_not: The flow is real but small, and it has shrunk since 2023 (−23 bp a trade after costs). Costs of about 28 bp a round trip leave nothing.
rows.mind: Cheaper execution, or an unseen period where the spread stays above 28 bp.
rows.citation: Harvey, C., Mazzoleni, M. & Melone, A. (2025). The Unintended Consequences of Rebalancing. NBER Working Paper 33554.

rows.name: Aggregate insider buying
rows.why: The signal worked around 2009 and has been close to zero since.
rows.expected: When company insiders buy their own stock across the market, returns tend to be higher afterwards. A market-level signal can be traded with one ETF.
rows.how: We built the signal from SEC insider filings since 2006 and tilted the book's equity ETFs with it. A separate test used it to time SPY.
rows.happened: Book Sharpe moved from 1.178 to 1.184, with only a 0.80 chance of a real gain (we need 0.90). Timing SPY earned 0.79 against 1.00 for holding it.
rows.why_not: Almost all of the signal's power came in 2009, when insiders bought the bottom. Since then it has had about no link to next month's returns.
rows.mind: A second market bottom where insider buying leads the turn.
rows.citation: Lakonishok, J. & Lee, I. (2001). Are Insider Trades Informative? Review of Financial Studies 14(1).

rows.name: Crash-probability overlay
rows.why: No model predicted the book's worst months better than their base rate.
rows.expected: If a model can tell when the book's worst months are coming, cutting exposure ahead of them would raise Sharpe.
rows.how: We labelled a month as a crash when the book's next 21-day return fell below its 5th percentile so far. XGBoost and a logistic model forecast it from volatility, the VIX curve, correlation and geopolitical risk.
rows.happened: There were only 183 crash days from 2012 to 2023. XGBoost's skill was −0.5% against the base rate, and the overlay had a 0.27 chance of helping.
rows.why_not: Crashes are rare, so there is too little to learn from. Calibrating the model on so few events made it worse.
rows.mind: A model that beats the base rate on a long, independent history of crashes.
rows.citation: Caldara, D. & Iacoviello, M. (2022). Measuring Geopolitical Risk. American Economic Review 112(4).

rows.name: Cross-asset momentum spillover
rows.why: It replicated on old US data and faded after 2014.
rows.expected: Past bond returns predict stock returns and past stock returns predict bond returns, in the opposite direction. Adding those signals to trend should help.
rows.how: We replicated the paper on US data from 1980, then blended the cross-asset signals into the book's trend sleeve.
rows.happened: It replicated through 2016, but the pair's Sharpe fell to 0.18 after 2014. In the book, Sharpe dropped from 1.178 to 1.096.
rows.why_not: The effect weakened after it was published, and the book's own trend signals already carry most of it.
rows.mind: The effect returning in data after 2026.
rows.citation: Pitkäjärvi, A., Suominen, M. & Vaittinen, L. (2020). Cross-asset signals and time series momentum. Journal of Financial Economics 136(1).

rows.name: Bond carry from the Fed's curve
rows.why: It agreed with the book's simple yield-curve switch on 97% of days.
rows.expected: Carry for each bond fund, measured as yield plus roll-down at its own maturity, should beat the book's single 10-year minus 3-month switch.
rows.how: We computed each fund's carry from the Fed's daily yield curve and used it in place of the switch. A second version added a credit tilt.
rows.happened: The per-fund signal matched the switch on 97% of days, and Sharpe went from 1.178 to 1.170.
rows.why_not: At these maturities the yield curve's slope already tells you almost everything carry does. A more exact measure of the same thing changed almost no trades.
rows.mind: A period where the funds' carry signs disagree with the curve's slope for months.
rows.citation: Koijen, R., Moskowitz, T., Pedersen, L. H. & Vrugt, E. (2018). Carry. Journal of Financial Economics 127(2).

rows.name: Correlation-aware trend sizing
rows.why: The gain came from lower volatility, and it was worse in 2008 and 2022.
rows.expected: Long SPY, EFA and VGK counts as three trend bets, though it is nearly one. Sizing by correlation should spread risk better.
rows.how: We replaced the trend sleeve's sizing with equal risk contribution, and in a second version with hierarchical risk parity.
rows.happened: Sharpe rose from 1.178 to 1.199 with equal risk contribution, and fell to 1.064 with hierarchical risk parity. Both did worse in 2022 and in 2008–09.
rows.why_not: The higher Sharpe came from running less risk, not from earning more. In the crises that matter most it lost more than the simple sizing.
rows.mind: A version that improves the crisis windows, not just the average.
rows.citation: Baltas, N. (2015). Trend-Following, Risk-Parity and the Influence of Correlations. In Risk-Based and Factor Investing, Elsevier.

rows.name: Intraday data in the vol forecast
rows.why: 5-minute data helped in calm years and under-forecast the 2020 and 2022 shocks.
rows.expected: Realised volatility from 5-minute returns measures today's risk far more precisely than daily returns. Most of the published gain in vol forecasting comes from this input.
rows.how: We built forecasts from 5-minute Alpaca data since 2016, first on their own and then as extra inputs to 2.1's model. Both were scored against 2.1's forecast from 2018.
rows.happened: The intraday inputs beat 2.1's forecast by 1.6% outside 2020 but lost by 33.6% in stress windows. Over the whole period they were 19.8% worse.
rows.why_not: Intraday measures react fast to calm, then extrapolate too little when a shock starts. 2.1's daily inputs, including the VIX curve, already cover what they add.
rows.mind: An intraday model that holds up in a stress window it wasn't trained on.
rows.citation: Andersen, T., Bollerslev, T., Diebold, F. & Labys, P. (2003). Modeling and Forecasting Realized Volatility. Econometrica 71(2).

rows.name: Vol forecast built on HAR
rows.why: A better forecast on paper, and a slightly worse book.
rows.expected: The standard HAR model plus forward-looking inputs, like data-release dates, might forecast volatility as well as 2.1's model with fewer parts.
rows.how: We combined HAR with XGBoost and tested the combination in the book from 2012 to 2023.
rows.happened: The forecast beat the 60-day window by 27.6%. In the book, Sharpe was 0.882 against 0.898 without it.
rows.why_not: The extra inputs added nothing a linear model could use, and the combination over-corrected in shock windows.
rows.mind: A version that beats 2.1's forecast in the book, not only on the forecast score.
rows.citation: Corsi, F. (2009). A Simple Approximate Long-Memory Model of Realized Volatility. Journal of Financial Econometrics 7(2).

rows.name: Battery day-ahead forecast
rows.why: The average daily price shape of the last 14 days beat every forecast on both grids.
rows.expected: A 1 MW, 4-hour battery earns by charging when power is cheap and selling when it's dear. A price forecast should pick the hours better than simple rules.
rows.how: We planned each day's charging the day before on ERCOT and CAISO prices, with weather as it was forecast at the time. v48 then put a residual model on top of the 14-day shape.
rows.happened: The 14-day shape captured 82.9% of perfect insight in ERCOT and 97.1% in CAISO, more than the forecast. The residual model on top of it scored −0.14 in ERCOT and −0.63 in CAISO.
rows.why_not: The money comes from a daily price shape that repeats, so an average of recent days already holds most of it. What's left is in rare spike days a forecast can't see coming.
rows.mind: A forecast archive long enough to test spike days, which would take years to build.
rows.citation: Salles, M., Huang, J., Aziz, M. & Hogan, W. (2017). Potential Arbitrage Revenue of Energy Storage Systems in PJM. Energies 10(8).

rows.name: VIX curve inversion trigger
rows.why: It switched late, re-risked into rebounds and tripled the overlay's trading.
rows.expected: When front-month VIX futures trade above the second month, the market is pricing near-term stress. That might be a faster de-risk signal than SPY's trend and volatility.
rows.how: We built our own VIX futures curve from Cboe settlements and used inversion as the de-risk trigger, with the same size and lag as the live rule.
rows.happened: Sharpe fell from 1.242 to 1.122, and the overlay traded 14.3 times a year instead of 4.8.
rows.why_not: The curve inverts and flips back within days around every spike. So it cut after the first drop and restored exposure in the rebound, then cut again.
rows.mind: A trigger that stays inverted through a whole sell-off.
rows.citation: Cheng, I.-H. (2019). The VIX Premium. Review of Financial Studies 32(1).

rows.name: TLT month-end
rows.why: Real but small, and the book already holds TLT at most month-ends.
rows.expected: Bond index funds extend duration at each month-end, and Treasury volume runs much higher on the last day. Long bonds might earn a premium over those days.
rows.how: Buy TLT at the open two days before month-end and sell at the next month's first open, 7 bps a side, over 236 month-ends.
rows.happened: It averaged +27.3 bp a trade (t +2.91) before costs. Added to the book at 10% it moved Sharpe from 1.242 to 1.243.
rows.why_not: Costs take half of a small edge. Counted against the 9,500 calendar rules that have been mined, its deflated Sharpe is 0.005.
rows.mind: A larger month-end effect after costs in new data.
rows.citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (2024). End-of-Month Liquidity in the Treasury Market.

rows.name: Treasury auction pair
rows.why: Gross return was below cost even before paying for the hedge.
rows.expected: Treasury notes cheapen in the days before a scheduled auction and recover afterwards. A pair hedged with short-term Treasuries should capture the swing.
rows.how: We used 2,793 note and bond auctions from Treasury's records and traded IEF and TLT around them, hedged with SHY.
rows.happened: Every auction together averaged +3.9 bp a trade before costs, and new issues +13.5 bp. Both were below the 14 bp bar to continue.
rows.why_not: TLT moves about six and a half times as much as SHY, so the hedge means trading far more than the position. Costs ran near 107 bp against a few basis points of gain.
rows.mind: A cheaper hedge than short-term Treasury ETFs.
rows.citation: Lou, D., Yan, H. & Zhang, J. (2013). Anticipated and Repeated Shocks in Liquid Markets. Review of Financial Studies 26(8).

rows.name: Agriculture curve proxy
rows.why: It earned what plain momentum earns, and sugar carried it.
rows.expected: In agricultural futures, the change in the curve's slope predicts returns beyond plain momentum. With no free contract data, we tested a proxy built from fund prices.
rows.how: Corn, soybeans, wheat and sugar from 2011, at an 8% volatility target with realistic roll costs. We set 2 trials in advance.
rows.happened: Net Sharpe was 0.22, the same as 12-month momentum on the same markets. Sugar made 97% of the profit while wheat lost 61%.
rows.why_not: There was no grain curve premium to pay for, and the book already runs a trend sleeve.
rows.mind: The free contract archive holding enough curve history to run the real test, around 2028.
rows.citation: Boons, M. & Prado, M. P. (2019). Basis-Momentum. Journal of Finance 74(1).

rows.name: Graph-clustering stat-arb (replication)
rows.why: A paper claimed 49% a year. With real fills it never traded its short leg.
rows.expected: A 2024 paper reported 49% a year from clustering S&P 500 stocks with a signed-graph method and trading short-term reversals inside each cluster.
rows.how: We ran it with the paper's own settings, then with clean prices, next-morning fills at 7 bps and a classifier retrained each year. SPY stood in for the missing short leg.
rows.happened: With the paper's settings it made −0.3% a year and traded on 4 of 228 rebalances. Hedged with SPY, it lost 12.5% a year (Sharpe −1.24).
rows.why_not: The classifier learned the market's upward drift and stopped trusting short signals. The paper's two best tickers were symbols later reused by other companies.
rows.mind: The authors' code reproducing their result on clean prices.
rows.citation: Korniejczuk, A. & Ślepaczuk, R. (2024). Statistical arbitrage in multi-pair trading strategy based on graph clustering algorithms in US equities market. arXiv 2406.10695.

rows.name: Stock-bond regime filter
rows.why: It changed the de-risk decision on 1.9% of days, and almost nothing else.
rows.expected: The de-risk rule might work better if it only fired when stocks and bonds fall together, when a book like this is most exposed.
rows.how: We added the stock-bond condition to the live overlay, judged against bars we set in advance.
rows.happened: It changed the decision on 110 of 5,815 days. Sharpe went from 1.193 to 1.201 and the worst drawdown didn't move.
rows.why_not: The sell-offs it was meant to pick out were mostly ones the simple rule already caught. An extra part that changes nothing is a cost.
rows.mind: A sell-off the simple rule misses and the filter catches.
rows.citation: Baltas, N. & Kosowski, R. (2020). Demystifying Time-Series Momentum Strategies. SSRN 2140091.

rows.name: Deep-RL volatility agent
rows.why: Fed properly, it held almost exactly equal weights.
rows.expected: A reinforcement-learning agent might learn when to shift risk between assets better than a fixed rule.
rows.how: We ran a PPO agent on the live paper track from June to October 2026, through the same broker as every strategy.
rows.happened: Once a data bug was fixed, its weights stayed within 1.7% of equal weight.
rows.why_not: It learned that the safest answer is to spread risk evenly, which a one-line rule does for free. We retired it in October 2026.
rows.mind: An agent that learns weights a simple rule can't match, out of sample.
rows.citation: Schulman, J., Wolski, F., Dhariwal, P., Radford, A. & Klimov, O. (2017). Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. arXiv 1707.06347.

rows.name: Calm-market leverage
rows.why: Levering up in quiet markets cut Sharpe from 1.22 to 0.86.
rows.expected: If the book is safer in calm markets, running it at higher leverage then should raise returns without much extra risk.
rows.how: We set leverage from trailing volatility and applied it the next day, on the meta-labelled book from 2007.
rows.happened: Sharpe fell from 1.22 to 0.86.
rows.why_not: Calm stretches end suddenly, so the rule was most levered when each sell-off began. Cutting exposure after markets turn works; adding it before they do concentrates the tail risk.
rows.mind: A calm-market signal that also warns before the calm ends.
rows.citation: Moreira, A. & Muir, T. (2017). Volatility-Managed Portfolios. Journal of Finance 72(4).

rows.name: LSTM features
rows.why: Its small lift came from look-ahead and vanished walk-forward.
rows.expected: A neural network trained on price histories might learn features the hand-built ones miss, and feed them to the meta-label model.
rows.how: We first pretrained it once on the whole history, then retrained it at each date on past data only.
rows.happened: Pretrained on everything, it lifted Sharpe from 1.226 to 1.242. Trained on the past only, Sharpe was 1.222.
rows.why_not: A 2010 feature from a model that had seen 2020 is look-ahead. Without it the network added nothing.
rows.mind: A walk-forward lift that holds in the forward record.
rows.citation: Hochreiter, S. & Schmidhuber, J. (1997). Long Short-Term Memory. Neural Computation 9(8).

rows.name: Currency trend
rows.why: Sharpe 0.15 on its own, and it lowered the book's.
rows.expected: Trend following works in currencies too, and a currency sleeve should diversify a book that is mostly stocks and bonds.
rows.how: Six currency ETFs from 2007, on the same engine as the book's trend sleeve. We tried 8 variants.
rows.happened: The best variant earned a Sharpe of 0.148, with a deflated Sharpe of 0. As a third sleeve it lowered the book's Sharpe.
rows.why_not: Currency trends have been weak since about 2010, while developed-market rates sat close together near zero.
rows.mind: Rates diverging across countries for long enough to make currency trends pay again.
rows.citation: Moskowitz, T., Ooi, Y. H. & Pedersen, L. H. (2012). Time Series Momentum. Journal of Financial Economics 104(2).

rows.name: Cointegrated pairs
rows.why: Only the strictest of five filters made money, and it left almost nothing to trade.
rows.expected: Two stocks whose prices move together should drift back when they separate. The trade is market-neutral, so it should diversify the book.
rows.how: Same-sector S&P 500 pairs from 2013, five variants set before the run, from loosest to strictest.
rows.happened: The four looser variants lost money after costs. The strictest earned a Sharpe of 0.23 with a 41% drawdown.
rows.why_not: Filtering hard enough to make it pay left too few trades to be worth the risk.
rows.mind: A pair universe outside the S&P 500, where spreads are wider.
rows.citation: Gatev, E., Goetzmann, W. & Rouwenhorst, K. G. (2006). Pairs Trading. Review of Financial Studies 19(3).

rows.name: S&P stock momentum
rows.why: Sharpe 0.17 after costs, against 0.91 for buy-and-hold.
rows.expected: Stocks that rose most over the past year tend to keep outperforming for a few months. It is the strongest single-stock anomaly on record.
rows.how: Point-in-time S&P 500 members from 2013, monthly rebalance at the next open, 7 bps.
rows.happened: Net Sharpe was 0.17. An earlier run looked good because of five corrupted price days in 2010 and 2011.
rows.why_not: Two decades after publication it is widely traded, and inside the S&P 500 winners and losers sit close together. The spread is small next to the cost of turning the book over.
rows.mind: A cleaner, broader universe like small caps, which free data doesn't cover.
rows.citation: Jegadeesh, N. & Titman, S. (1993). Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers. Journal of Finance 48(1).

rows.name: Post-earnings drift
rows.why: Market beta, not drift. Alpha after the market was −3.25% a year.
rows.expected: After a large earnings surprise, prices tend to keep drifting the same way for weeks.
rows.how: We traded in the direction of big S&P 500 earnings gaps from 2021 and held for up to 45 trading days.
rows.happened: Net Sharpe was 0.25, but its beta to SPY was 0.36. After removing that, alpha was −3.25% a year.
rows.why_not: Most of its return came from holding stocks while the market rose. Holding 0.36 of the index would have done better with fewer trades.
rows.mind: Positive alpha in a falling market.
rows.citation: Bernard, V. & Thomas, J. (1989). Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift. Journal of Accounting Research 27.

rows.name: S&P short-term reversal
rows.why: The original engine. Once three simulator bugs were fixed, it lost money.
rows.expected: Stocks that fell most over the last few days tend to bounce. This was the engine the project started with.
rows.how: Point-in-time S&P 500 members from 2014, beta-neutral, next-day open, 7 bps. Between v26 and v28 we fixed three bugs in our own simulator first.
rows.happened: Sharpe was −0.08 with a 56% drawdown. The bugs had made four sleeves look good, and the combined book fell from 0.63 to 0.11 once they were fixed.
rows.why_not: The edge lasts a few days, so the book turns over many times a year and pays 7 bps each way. In the most traded stocks in the world, the bounce is smaller than that.
rows.mind: A cost per trade well below 7 bps.
rows.citation: Lehmann, B. (1990). Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency. Quarterly Journal of Economics 105(1).

rows.name: The original TGA engine
rows.why: Its +0.60 Sharpe vanished when the price data was re-downloaded.
rows.expected: Graph-topology and reversal signals on S&P 500 stocks, with a classifier gate and Kelly sizing, could earn a daily edge.
rows.how: Built and tuned from v10 to v24, before we kept a trial ledger, on one copy of the price data.
rows.happened: When the price data was re-downloaded with 831 tickers instead of 768, the base rule went from −0.04 to −0.15. Its own alpha was indistinguishable from zero.
rows.why_not: A result that changes with the ticker list is an artifact of the data. The +0.60 came from its momentum leg.
rows.mind: The same result on two independent copies of the data.
rows.citation: Lo, A. & MacKinlay, A. C. (1990). When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction? Review of Financial Studies 3(2).

rows.name: Intraday momentum
rows.why: The first half-hour didn't predict the last half-hour in SPY, QQQ or IWM.
rows.expected: The first half-hour's return predicts the last half-hour's, partly because leveraged ETFs rebalance near the close.
rows.how: We measured it on 1-minute bars from 2016 before writing any trading rule. To go on, the slope needed a t-stat of at least 2 and to be positive in 6 of 11 years.
rows.happened: SPY's slope was +0.017 (t 0.59), positive in 4 of 11 years. QQQ and IWM were no better.
rows.why_not: If the effect existed, it is gone from the most traded ETFs. We stopped before any trial.
rows.mind: The slope showing up in a later sample.
rows.citation: Gao, L., Han, Y., Li, S. Z. & Zhou, G. (2018). Market Intraday Momentum. Journal of Financial Economics 129(2).

rows.name: China's activity from space (NO2)
rows.why: China's data moves copper, but satellite NO2 didn't predict that data.
rows.expected: China buys about half the world's copper. Satellite NO2 over its factories might read industrial activity before official data, and copper and the Australian dollar would follow.
rows.how: We checked each link in turn, from official data to prices, then NO2 to official data from 1996, then a timing trade.
rows.happened: Official surprises did move the assets (t 2.47). NO2 called the surprise's sign 54.7% of the time, and the trade lost (net Sharpe −0.62).
rows.why_not: The middle link failed: monthly NO2 is too noisy to predict official activity. A weekly archive keeps running for a forward record.
rows.mind: Weekly NO2 that predicts the official release in the forward record.
rows.citation: European Space Agency, Copernicus Sentinel-5P and KNMI/TEMIS tropospheric NO2 products.

rows.name: Macro momentum in country equities
rows.why: Countries with improving economies beat the rest until about 2014, not after.
rows.expected: Countries whose growth is rising and inflation falling should beat the rest over the next month. Satellite NO2 might read growth before official data.
rows.how: We used the OECD's data as it was first published, on country ETFs from 2006. NO2 was measured first, as a nowcast.
rows.happened: Net Sharpe was −0.10, positive until about 2014 and negative after. NO2 called the direction of growth 49.9% of the time.
rows.why_not: The premium decayed after the research that found it, and NO2 added nothing. We stopped at the first test.
rows.mind: The premium coming back in data after 2026.
rows.citation: Brooks, J. (2017). A Half Century of Macro Momentum. AQR Capital Management.

rows.name: Country value and carry
rows.why: Cheap, high-yield countries stopped beating expensive ones after 2014.
rows.expected: Countries whose markets are cheap and pay high dividends should beat expensive, low-yield ones over the next month.
rows.how: We first replicated the published value factor on country indices from 1981, before writing any ETF code.
rows.happened: Net Sharpe was 0.04 over the full history and −0.31 from 2014. The published factor itself turned negative from 2014.
rows.why_not: The premium decayed after it was published. The replication matched exactly, so it isn't a data error.
rows.mind: Value returning in country indices for several years.
rows.citation: Asness, C., Moskowitz, T. & Pedersen, L. H. (2013). Value and Momentum Everywhere. Journal of Finance 68(3).

rows.name: VIX futures premium timing
rows.why: Its first test failed. The signal faded after 2014.
rows.expected: VIX futures usually trade above spot VIX and drift down toward it. Two published rules short them when that gap is wide.
rows.how: We tested whether the gap still predicted futures returns after the papers' sample, before running any trading rule.
rows.happened: After July 2014 the slope was +0.0098 (t +1.28), the wrong sign. The 3 rules were never run.
rows.why_not: What's left is the plain volatility premium, which loses in the same crashes as equities. That's the opposite of what this book needs.
rows.mind: The gap predicting returns again in new data.
rows.citation: Simon, D. P. & Campasano, J. (2014). The VIX Futures Basis. Journal of Derivatives 21(3).

rows.name: Claude News Overlay
rows.why: Built and paused before any trial, to rule out look-ahead first.
rows.expected: A language model reading only news published before each date might add information the price-based de-risk rule lacks.
rows.how: We built a point-in-time news archive from October 2025, after the model's training cutoff, with pinned models.
rows.happened: No trials ran. About a year of history is clean, too short to judge a strategy.
rows.why_not: A model trained to August 2025 has read about everything before then, so any earlier backtest is contaminated.
rows.mind: A forward record long enough to judge.
rows.citation: Lopez-Lira, A. & Tang, Y. (2023). Can ChatGPT Forecast Stock Price Movements? SSRN 4412788.
